L4@P0: HRA-Secure Homomorphic Lattice-Based Proxy
L5@P0: Re-Encryption with Tight Security
L6@P0: Aloni Cohen1, David Bruce Cousins2, Nicholas Genisea, 3,
L7@P0: Erik Kline4, Yuriy Polyakovb, 2 and Saraswathy RVc
L8@P0: 1 University of Chicago, USA

L12@P0: Abstract. We construct an efficient proxy re-encryption (PRE) scheme secure against
L13@P0: honest re-encryption attacks (HRA-secure) with precise concrete security estimates.
L14@P0: To get these precise concrete security estimates, we introduce the tight, fine-grained
L15@P0: noise-flooding techniques of Li et al. (CRYPTO’22) to RLWE-based (homomorphic)
L16@P0: PRE schemes, as well as a mixed statistical-computational security definition to
L17@P0: HRA security analysis. Our solution also supports homomorphic operations on the
L18@P0: ciphertexts. Such homomorphism allows for advanced applications, e.g., encrypted
L19@P0: computation of network statistics across networks, and unlimited hops in the case of
L20@P0: full homomorphism, i.e., when bootstrapping is available.
L21@P0: We implement our PRE scheme in the OpenFHE software library and apply it to a
L22@P0: problem of secure multi-hop data distribution in the context of 5G virtual network
L23@P0: slices. We also experimentally evaluate the performance of our scheme, demonstrating
L24@P0: that the implementation is practical.
L25@P0: Moreover, we compare our PRE method with other lattice-based PRE schemes and
L26@P0: approaches targeting HRA security. These achieve HRA security, but not in a tight,
L27@P0: practical scheme such as our work. Further, we present an attack on the PRE scheme
L28@P0: proposed in Davidson et al.’s (ACISP’19), which was claimed to achieve HRA security
L29@P0: without noise flooding, i.e., without adding large noise.
L30@P0: Keywords: Lattice-Based Proxy Re-Encryption · Homomorphic Encryption · Distributed Networking
L31@P0: 1 Introduction
L32@P0: Proxy re-encryption (PRE), introduced by Blaze, Bleumer, and Strauss [BBS98], allows
L33@P0: re-encrypting ciphertexts encrypted under a secret key to a new encryption of the same
L34@P0: message under a different secret key without ever having to decrypt the ciphertext. That
L35@P0: is, PRE schemes allow for local delegation of keys. Such schemes have been studied for
L36@P0: a wide variety of applications such as encrypted email forwarding, key escrow [Coh19],
L37@P0: encrypted file storage [AFGH06], secure payment system for credit cards [GLSW21],
L38@P0: sharing patient medical records with emergency care providers [PRSV17, BGP+17], and
L39@P0: access control for data sharing in IoT [DCN18, ZPW+15]. Multi-hop PRE is a chain of
L40@P0: multiple re-encryptions from a source to a destination where a hop refers to a re-encryption.
L41@P0: For example, multi-hop PRE solves such problems associated with distributing sensitive
L42@P0: E-mail: aloni@uchicago.edu (Aloni Cohen), ypolyakov@dualitytech.com (Yuriy Polyakov)
L43@P0: aThis work was done while this author was at Duality Technologies Inc.
L44@P0: bCorresponding author
L45@P0: cThis work was done while this author was at Duality Technologies Inc.

L47@P0-1: Received: 2025-01-10 Accepted: 2025-03-112 HRA-Secure Lattice-Based PRE
L48@P1: information payloads within and across trust boundaries while limiting distribution of
L49@P1: encryption keys to within the boundaries of a trust zone, or to pairwise interactions
L50@P1: between trusted agents across trust zone boundaries.
L51@P1: On the security side, many PRE schemes are cryptographically secure from users
L52@P1: outside the network (without secret keys) under chosen plaintext attacks (IND-CPA),
L53@P1: akin to many public-key encryption schemes. However, most applications necessitate
L54@P1: security from adversaries within the network since otherwise all users in a network would
L55@P1: simply share a single symmetric key. One prominent example of the need for security
L56@P1: against internal adversaries is in 5G virtual network slices [ON20], where a virtual network
L57@P1: operator’s (VNO) leased hardware can leak intermediate ciphertexts via side-channel
L58@P1: attacks. Then, an adversary can see the intermediate ciphertext, before re-encryption,
L59@P1: as well as the re-encrypted ciphertext under their secret key. Despite sounding harmless,
L60@P1: this simple attack can lead to secret key recovery attacks between users in the network.
L61@P1: Cohen [Coh19] showed IND-CPA security does not suffice in this setting and developed
L62@P1: honest re-encryption (HRA) security for PRE to be robust against honest-but-curious
L63@P1: users within the network. Notably, Cohen showed that all prior PRE schemes based on
L64@P1: the (Ring)-Learning-With-Errors problem [Reg05, LPR10], (R)LWE, notably [PRSV17],
L65@P1: suffer from honest-but-curious adversaries being able to recover the ciphertext’s RLWE
L66@P1: error which then allows for learning the secret key by solving a linear system of equations.
L67@P1: Shortly after Cohen’s work [Coh19], Li and Micciancio [LM21] applied a very similar
L68@P1: RLWE attack to an approximate FHE scheme, namely, the Cheon–Kim–Kim–Song (CKKS)
L69@P1: scheme [CKKS17], where the adversary gets a somewhat restricted decryption oracle,
L70@P1: introduced as part of a new IND-CPAD security definition [LM21, Definition 2]. The
L71@P1: underlying implication of this connection is that the (R)LWE schemes for PRE are deeply
L72@P1: connected to the (R)LWE schemes for (approximate) FHE. Both Cohen’s fix for (R)LWE
L73@P1: PRE schemes and the fix for CKKS require some form of noise flooding [LMSS22], but the
L74@P1: latter introduced a fine-grained flooding technique for optimal parameters mixing both
L75@P1: statistical and computational security, whereas the former relied on loose, theoretical noise
L76@P1: flooding bounds [AJL+12]. Therefore, there is currently a significant gap in the state of
L77@P1: the art in concrete security for approximate and threshold FHE compared to the state of
L78@P1: the art in concrete security for lattice-based PRE schemes.
L79@P1: Lattice-based PRE schemes must be practical since they are the only class of PRE
L80@P1: schemes resistant to quantum attacks. For example, lattice-based schemes were recently
L81@P1: chosen by the National Institute of Standards (NIST) for standardized digital signatures
L82@P1: and key-exchange mechanisms1. A simple quantum attack is the “harvest now, decrypt
L83@P1: later” attack, where an adversary stores ciphertexts now and decrypts them once they
L84@P1: have access to a quantum computer. Post-quantum, hence lattice-based, schemes are
L85@P1: cryptographic schemes robust against these attacks.
L86@P1: In addition, a notable feature of RLWE schemes is that they support homomorphism
L87@P1: and the popular fully-homomorphic encryption (FHE) schemes are based on RLWE.
L88@P1: These include the Brakerski/Fan–Vercauteren (BFV) [Bra12, FV12] and Brakerski-GentryVaikuntanathan (BGV) [BGV14] schemes, two schemes in the simultaneous-instructionmultiple-data (SIMD) paradigm with the same plaintext spaces. FHE in the context of
L89@P1: proxy-re-encryption enables delegating computation and key responsibilities to the cloud.
L90@P1: FHE-based PRE schemes also enable an unlimited number of hops in the multi-hop setting
L91@P1: since one can bootstrap a ciphertext en-route whenever the noise budget diminishes after
L92@P1: so many hops.
L93@P1-2: 1https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/post-quantum-cryptography/selected-algorithms-2022Cohen et al. 3
L94@P2: 1.1 Our Contributions
L95@P2: We introduce the tight, rigorously secure noise flooding technique recently proposed by Li
L96@P2: et al. [LMSS22] for approximate homomorphic encryption to lattice-based PRE schemes
L97@P2: with HRA security. This fine-grained noise flooding yields a procedure used for erasing
L98@P2: the information about the previous secret key after re-encryption in PRE schemes. We
L99@P2: propose an efficient, provable, HRA-secure PRE scheme with precise security estimates
L100@P2: by introducing a mixed, statistical-computational security definition and analysis. We
L101@P2: build our system on top of the BGV FHE scheme, enabling PRE schemes with full
L102@P2: homomorphism and unlimited re-encryptions. The same underlying ideas can be extended
L103@P2: to BFV and CKKS FHE schemes as well.
L104@P2: We provide an efficient implementation of the PRE scheme using the OpenFHE library,
L105@P2: which implements all common FHE schemes [ABB+22]. We also implement a networking
L106@P2: application system (motivated by a use case in 5G virtual network slice security) based
L107@P2: on the PRE functionality with Google’s RPC framework [Goo] for multiple hops where
L108@P2: an AES symmetric key is the data payload. We perform network simulation using the
L109@P2: open-source RAVEN framework [Ins]. For the single-hop setting, the re-encryption time in
L110@P2: OpenFHE on an Intel® CoreTM i7-9700 CPU with 64 GB RAM, a commodity desktop
L111@P2: machine, for our HRA-secure PRE scheme is about 2 milliseconds. The timing for a 13-hop
L112@P2: parameter set starts with 103 milliseconds for re-encrypting a fresh 6.5MB ciphertext,
L113@P2: and ultimately drops down to 32 milliseconds for the last (13th) hop. Our PRE scheme
L114@P2: implementation is publicly available as part of the OpenFHE library [ABB+22]. Our
L115@P2: networking application system implementation is also publicly available in a separate
L116@P2: OpenFHE project repository [Dua].
L117@P2: In addition, we explore lattice-based alternatives to our approach for achieving HRA
L118@P2: security. In particular, we examine the divide-and-round technique of de Castro et
L119@P2: al. [dCJV21] used to achieve circuit privacy in homomorphic encryption schemes. We
L120@P2: conclude this technique does not allow a more efficient multi-hop HRA-secure scheme.
L121@P2: Furthermore, we show that the scheme presented in [DDLM19], which uses simple ciphertext
L122@P2: re-randomization (adding small encryption noise) without noise flooding, i.e., without
L123@P2: adding large noise, is not HRA-secure despite their claims. (See Appendices B and C for
L124@P2: more details.)
L125@P2: Connections to threshold and approximate FHE. Our work is closely related to
L126@P2: the state of the art in threshold FHE [AJL+12, KS23] and approximate FHE [LMSS22]
L127@P2: since (R)LWE-based PRE, approximate FHE, and threshold FHE all compute some form
L128@P2: of approximate decryption, or the decryption function without rounding. In PRE, this
L129@P2: is achieved through key switching, enabled by (R)LWE’s key homomorphism. Because
L130@P2: the decryption error is not rounded away during re-encryption, as in the full RLWE
L131@P2: decryption algorithm, the new ciphertext carries the old ciphertext’s error. We construct
L132@P2: an optimal scheme based on the state of the art in concrete security of this approximate
L133@P2: decryption phenomenon. One could, however, round away the error at each hop, but this
L134@P2: requires the inefficient bootstrapping procedure in FHE. (See Gentry’s thesis [Gen09] for
L135@P2: more information on PRE using bootstrapping.) Our work shows how these three areas,
L136@P2: RLWE-based PRE, approximate FHE, and threshold FHE, are deeply connected. In short,
L137@P2: an advancement in one of these areas yields an advance in the others.
L138@P2: 1.2 Related work
L139@P2: Our work improves upon the Polyakov–Rohloff–Sahu–Vaikuntanathan (PRSV) [BGP+17,
L140@P2: PRSV17] system whose underlying PRE scheme does not provide HRA security. We
L141@P2: fix this by applying the fine-grained noise flooding technique of [LMSS22] (used in the
L142@P2: context of approximate FHE) to RLWE-based PRE schemes. This technique breaks any
L143@P2-3: correlations among ciphertexts and former secret keys (as part of re-encryption) and4 HRA-Secure Lattice-Based PRE
L144@P3: provides a tight security reduction. The resulting scheme is multi-hop, uni-directional
L145@P3: (re-encryption is one-way), and the initial ciphertext grows with the number of hops due
L146@P3: to the noise flooding technique, while the re-encrypted ciphertext size drops at every hop
L147@P3: due to modulus switching.
L148@P3: Attribute-based encryption (ABE) is another possible solution to building an encrypted,
L149@P3: distributed-trust system in a network. ABE is a generalization of identity-based encryption
L150@P3: (IBE) where the public key for encryption is created using a set of attributes defined by an
L151@P3: access policy. The access policy determines which consumers can access data published by
L152@P3: a producer. ABE is more appropriate for cloud systems where many users try to decrypt
L153@P3: the same ciphertext rather than for point-to-point communication. Many ABE schemes
L154@P3: based on bilinear pairings have been proposed in the literature [dlPVA22] but are not
L155@P3: post-quantum. Lattice-based ABE schemes are not efficient [DDP+18, GPR+19, GMP19]
L156@P3: but offer richer access policies than PRE. For example, the runtimes presented in Table
L157@P3: 2 of [DDP+18] (for a very small number of Boolean attributes and binary messages) are
L158@P3: significantly larger (often by orders of magnitude) than the PRE runtimes (for much larger
L159@P3: messages) shown in Tables 2 and 4 of our paper.
L160@P3: Fine-grained PRE, first constructed by Zhou et al. [ZLHZ23] in the single-hop CPAsecure setting and later improved to the multi-hop HRA setting [ZLH24], are PRE schemes
L161@P3: where the message, m, gets transformed to a known function, f(m). The constructions in
L162@P3: [ZLHZ23, ZLH24] are based on lattice trapdoors [GPV08, MP12], similar to the state-ofthe-art ABE schemes. Therefore, these schemes are interesting from a theoretical point of
L163@P3: view but suffer the same practical efficiency issues faced by lattice-based ABE schemes.
L164@P3: Neither [ZLHZ23] nor [ZLH24] provide an implementation or give practical parameters2.
L165@P3: Our work improves these schemes on three fronts: 1) we offer arbitrary homomorphism, 2)
L166@P3: a tight security reduction and optimized parameters, and 3) practical implementation and
L167@P3: simplicity of design. Practical deployments of PRE must be constant-time, and making
L168@P3: our scheme constant-time (as we sample a discrete gaussian on Z
L169@P3: N ) is much simpler than
L170@P3: making discrete gaussian sampling constant time in the trapdoor-lattice regime [MW17]
L171@P3: since the lattice in the latter setting is described by secret key, unlike Z
L172@P3: N .
L173@P3: HRA security is now the standard in PRE schemes. The work in [DDLM19] presents
L174@P3: a PRE scheme as an extension of the scheme in [PRSV17] to achieve HRA security and
L175@P3: strong IND-post-compromise security (PCS). PCS ensures an adversary cannot distinguish
L176@P3: a re-encrypted ciphertext from random uniform assuming the re-encryption key is known
L177@P3: to the adversary and corruption of the producer’s (sender’s) secret. The re-encryption from
L178@P3: [PRSV17] is extended with a re-randomization of the ciphertext, but it does not use an
L179@P3: error distribution with sufficiently large standard deviation to flood traces of the previous
L180@P3: secret key from the ciphertext, making it prone to an averaging attack. This is because
L181@P3: the noise in the ciphertext is correlated to the sender’s secret. Refer to Appendix B for an
L182@P3: outlined HRA attack on [DDLM19] using binary matrix (R)LWE attacks [HM17] together
L183@P3: with an averaging attack.
L184@P3: Fuchsbauer et al. [FKKP19] achieve adaptively secure PRE, where the adversary
L185@P3: can corrupt any party throughout the security game, with a general reduction which
L186@P3: is exponential in a parameter which depends on the adversary’s corruptions, n
L187@P3: O(log n)
L188@P3: for a binary tree of corruptions and 2
L189@P3: O(n)
L190@P3: loss in general corruptions, where n is the
L191@P3: number of parties. Asymptotically, this super-polynomial loss in security makes the scheme
L192@P3: impractical for our use-case with many clients. As for concrete efficiency, their scheme
L193@P3: appears to be much slower than ours because the former uses ciphertext sanitation, i.e.,
L194@P3: multiple FHE bootstrappings [DS16], in addition to noise flooding, to achieve this for
L195@P3: lattice-based PRE schemes. They did not implement their scheme.
L196@P3: 2The parameter suggestions for security parameter λ = 128, lattice dimension 128 and ciphertext

L198@P3: 70 do not meet the lattice cryptography security estimates in the Homomorphic Encryption
L199@P3: Standard https://homomorphicencryption.org/standard/, for example. Therefore, these parameter
L200@P3-4: estimates are asymptotic.Cohen et al. 5
L201@P4: An even more powerful PRE scheme is universal PRE, where re-encryption is done
L202@P4: between any public key scheme. Döttling and Nishimaki [DN21] achieve this by using
L203@P4: either (probabilistic) indistinguishability obfuscation or garbled circuits over the PKE
L204@P4: schemes (not practically efficient).
L205@P4: Susilo et al. [SDDR21] show a lattice-based construction of attribute-based PRE. Their
L206@P4: construction used lattice-based ABE (lattice trapdoors) and is not implemented. We
L207@P4: expect their solution to be similar in computational and storage complexity to the state of
L208@P4: the art in lattice-based ABE.
L209@P4: PRE schemes based on the decisional bilinear Diffie–Hellman (DBDH) problem were
L210@P4: presented in [AFGH06, CH07, ID03]. The scheme in [AFGH06] is IND-CPA secure and
L211@P4: provides low performance run-times for 256 and 512 bits of classical security.
L212@P4: Several papers focused on noise flooding in threshold FHE. For example, Chowdhurry
L213@P4: et al. claimed they were able to develop the first practical TFHE scheme with a polynomial
L214@P4: modulus-to-noise ratio [CSS+22]. However, their claim was subsequently shown to be
L215@P4: incorrect (see the prior works discussion in [PS25] for more details). If more than one
L216@P4: round is allowed, flooding noise can be avoided using extra interactions during distributed
L217@P4: decryption [PS25]. Further details on the issue of noise flooding in threshold FHE schemes
L218@P4: are provided in [BGG+18, MBH23]. An extension of threshold FHE to threshold latticebased signatures is discussed in [GKS24].
L219@P4: 1.3 Organization
L220@P4: PRE and other background are reviewed in Section 2. Our PRE scheme is presented in
L221@P4: Section 3 with correctness and security analysis. Section 4 describes our network application.
L222@P4: The logic for setting the parameters is explained in Section 5. The experimental results
L223@P4: are presented in Section 6, followed by concluding remarks in Section 7. Appendix A
L224@P4: discusses the details of key switching and BGV scheme optimizations. Appendix B shows
L225@P4: the necessity of noise flooding in RLWE schemes based on the PRSV scheme. We explore
L226@P4: alternatives to noise flooding in Appendix C. The rest of the appendices discusses the
L227@P4: details of our implementation for the networking use case.

L307@P5: 2.2 Security under Honest Re-Encryption Attacks (HRA)
L308@P5: The IND-CPA security definition for PRE is adapted from the IND-CPA security definition
L309@P5: for encryption schemes. On a high level, it shows indistinguishability of re-encrypted
L310@P5: ciphertexts when the adversary is given access to a re-encryption key generation oracle
L311@P5: from corrupt to honest parties and corrupt to corrupt parties. (A party is corrupt if
L312@P5: the adversary knows this party’s secret key.) Cohen showed IND-CPA security is not
L313@P5: strong enough for most applications and introduced HRA-security [Coh19], a stronger
L314@P5: security definition modeled against an honest-but-curious adversary corrupting parties
L315@P5: with re-encryption keys. HRA security allows the adversary to query for re-encryption on
L316@P5: non-challenge ciphertexts from an honest key to a corrupted key as well, in addition to the
L317@P5-6: access allowed in the IND-CPA model.Cohen et al. 7
